clinicalPearls: A recurrent deletion mediated by non-allelic homologous recombination between the olfactory-receptor gene clusters (segmental duplications) that flank the interval
Congenital heart disease is a leading feature, especially atrioventricular septal defects and other septal lesions, linked to the GATA4 gene
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs in a proportion of cases
Developmental delay, mild to moderate intellectual disability and behavioural difficulties (including hyperactivity and impulsivity) are common
Microcephaly and variable facial dysmorphism may be present
The reciprocal duplication of the same region exists and has its own, generally milder, phenotype
Expressivity is variable and the change may be inherited from a mildly affected parent
Chromosomal microarray is the first-line diagnostic investigation
reference.pathophysiology: The 8p23.1 region is bordered by large clusters of olfactory-receptor genes that function as segmental duplications and predispose to non-allelic homologous recombination, producing a recurrent deletion or its reciprocal duplication. The interval contains dosage-sensitive developmental genes, notably GATA4, a transcription factor essential for cardiac septation and diaphragm formation; its haploinsufficiency largely accounts for the congenital heart disease and diaphragmatic hernia. Loss of additional genes in the region contributes to the neurodevelopmental and behavioural features. Variable expressivity reflects differences in deletion size and background genetic modifiers.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic causes of congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Other recurrent copy-number syndromes causing developmental delay and behavioural problems
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder without a copy-number change
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as first-line to detect and size the deletion
FISH or MLPA to confirm the deletion
Parental studies to establish inheritance and counsel recurrence risk
Echocardiography to define congenital heart disease
Chest imaging where diaphragmatic hernia is suspected
redFlags: Haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease requiring cardiology or surgical input
Respiratory distress suggestive of diaphragmatic hernia in the neonate
Severe behavioural disturbance affecting safety or schooling
reference.prognosis: Outlook is largely determined by the severity of the congenital heart disease and any diaphragmatic hernia; when these are corrected, many children do well with mild to moderate learning and behavioural difficulties. Neurodevelopmental support and cardiac follow-up shape long-term function.
pitfalls: Failing to arrange echocardiography given the strong association with congenital heart disease
Overlooking a diaphragmatic hernia presenting with respiratory symptoms
Assuming an inherited deletion is benign despite variable expressivity
Attributing behavioural problems solely to the deletion without appropriate assessment and support
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Surgical correction of the congenital heart disease, particularly atrioventricular and other septal defects linked to GATA4 haploinsufficiency, with paediatric cardiology follow-up
Surgical repair of congenital diaphragmatic hernia when present, supported by neonatal respiratory stabilisation
Developmental and behavioural intervention, including educational support for intellectual disability and behavioural strategies for hyperactivity and impulsivity
Echocardiographic and chest-imaging surveillance to define and monitor the structural anomalies
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across paediatric cardiology, neonatal and paediatric surgery, developmental paediatrics and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling with parental studies to establish inheritance and counsel recurrence risk
